intro: A subword tokenizer learns useful adjacent pairs from a corpus. Frequent words must contribute more evidence than rare words.
task: Count weighted adjacent token-pair occurrences across supplied word segmentations.
requirements: words is a nonempty list of token lists containing nonempty strings; individual token lists may be empty.
frequencies is a matching vector of nonnegative integer values. Count every adjacent occurrence, including overlapping occurrences.
Return a Python dictionary with two-string tuple keys and integer counts. Omit zero-total pairs. Do not join separate words.
Do not modify inputs. Raise ValueError for the invalid shapes, ranges, or non-finite numeric inputs described above. Numerical checks use moderate finite values unless stated otherwise.

hints.title: Choose the representation
hints.body: Visit each word with its frequency and zip the token list with itself shifted by one.

hints.title: Check the boundary
hints.body: Accumulate tuple keys directly; concatenated strings can confuse different token boundaries.

explanation: Byte-pair encoding repeatedly merges a frequent adjacent token pair. Pair statistics are weighted by word frequency so the model reflects the corpus, not merely a list of unique words.
Counting and merging have different overlap rules. The sequence a,a,a contains two adjacent a,a observations, even though a single left-to-right merge can consume only one of them.
Compare a common short word with a rare long word. Explain why unweighted pair counts can choose a different merge and produce a different vocabulary.
